title: Trump directs federal contractors to coordinate with White House on congressional requests for information | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

President Donald Trump has ordered federal contractors to notify the White House of any congressional requests for information on their work and to coordinate their responses with the administration — a move that Democrats say is unlawful as they prepare to launch investigations into his administration next year.

An executive order signed by the president Friday said contractors must “abide by any instructions received from the White House and contracting agency related to the withholding of communications that the White House or the agency has determined are protected by executive privilege.”

“If the executive branch cannot be assured that those communications will remain confidential, agencies and the White House will be chilled from sharing sensitive information with contractors, which will stymie the operation of critical Government programs,” the executive order argues.

The order warns contractors that their agreements with the federal government could be terminated if they fail to comply with its directives.

It also accuses certain congressional leaders of “harassing private companies that contract with the federal government” for information and reminds them that their probes must have a “valid legislative purpose.”

Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin, who is poised to chair the House Judiciary Committee when Democrats take control in January, called the executive order “unprecedented and blatantly unlawful.”

“Federal contractors are paid with taxpayer dollars, not Trump’s personal billions,” Raskin said in a statement Saturday. “Public contractors have both a duty and a right to speak truthfully when Congress calls, and Congress has a duty to investigate and stamp out all the waste, fraud, kickbacks, shakedowns and corruption choking the government and driving up costs. After two years of MAGA Republicans in Congress colluding with Trump Inc., accountability and the Rule of Law are coming.”

Democrats have mused aboutinvestigationsinto the work Trump has ordered across Washington, DC, including the construction of the White House ballroom, the repairs to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and the planned renovations of the Kennedy Center.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who will chair a key Senate investigative panel, earlier this monthsent lettersto a slew of companies asking them to cooperate with a planned inquiry into the ballroom. The Connecticut senator previously requested from the construction firm carrying out the projectinformation about the ballroom’s anticipated costand how it came to chosen as the builder.

Democrats have also said they will seek to address theinflux of contractsthe Department of Homeland Security has granted in Trump’s second term.

“Once we have control, then there’s a lot more we can do on guardrails,” Rep. Rep. Henry Cuellar, the ranking member on the House Appropriations Homeland Security subcommittee, has told CNN, referring to bringing the funds under his committee’s oversight.

While still in the minority in Congress, Democrats have sought to investigate the department’s controversial purchasing of planes and contracts to aid Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportation operations, as well ascontractsfor the construction of additional border wall inBig Bend National Park.

DHS also came under scrutiny last year afterProPublica reportedthat a firm run by the husband of the agency’s chief spokesperson, Tricia McLaughlin, was subcontracted to produce an advertising campaign for the department in a $200 million deal. McLaughlin told ProPublica at the time that DHS had no visibility into which subcontractors were selected and that she recused herself because of the conflict of interest.

Friday’s directive marks the latest guidance put out by the White House in anticipation of Democrats’ investigations. White House counsel Will Scharf last week penned a memo stating that executive agencies and departments within the Trump administration must obtain approval from the White House before any personnel agree to testify before Congress.

More broadly, the White House has taken acombative approachto the planned oversight of the administration. Scharf last week wrote Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, saying that the administration “will not be extortedand will not be cowed by unlawful process motivated by animus, pettiness, hatred, or any other unlawful motive to intimidate, penalize or interfere with the lawful functioning of government.”

In a separate letter to Democratic committee leaders, Scharf stated that Trump administration officials do not have to comply with demands to preserve or turn over records because of those Democrats’ current status in the congressional minority.

Garcia condemned the president’s order on Saturday.

“Today’s executive order is the latest in the Trump Administration’s blatant attack on Congress’ constitutional right to conduct oversight,” Garciasaid in a poston social media. “What is the White House trying to hide? Donald Trump wants to stop us from exposing the rampant waste, fraud, and corruption by his Administration, but we’re just getting started.”

Meanwhile, a top Congressional Democrat on Fridaywarned that lawmakers will withhold government fundingfor systems developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX if the Trump administration and tech billionaire refuse to disclose who is responsible for ordering the slowdown of Ukraine’s military-grade Starlink satellite service — the subject of another potential investigation next year.

This story was updated with new details.

CNN’s Priscilla Alvarez, Audrey Ash, Annie Grayer, Katelyn Polantz, Zachary Cohen and Tierney Sneed contributed to this report.
